nodes.title: Working with the specification
nodes.text: How the specification is kept and implemented.

children.title: The foundations
children.text: What the specification is made of and how it is changed.

children.title: The nodes are the specification
children.text:
The specification is the set of its nodes.

Whatever is generated from them — a readable export (for example, in markdown), the map, the instructions an agent reads — is regenerated after every change to them and never edited, and nothing is ever read back from it into the specification. What is generated from them into the system's code — its types and runtime checks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and what a project's own generators write (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze) — waits for its nodes instead: it is regenerated only once every node it is generated from is approved, and until then no commit changes it.

Where a generated copy is kept, it is checked against what the nodes produce, unless it waits.
children.reason:
A structure a schema can check is hard for a person to read, so a readable copy is needed; but a copy that is edited, fed back into the nodes or left behind them would be a second version of the rules: sooner or later one version would change and the other not, and whoever read the unchanged one would implement a rule that no longer holds. Regenerated by the tools at every change and checked against the nodes, a copy is a view of the one source rather than a second one.

Code generated from a node is part of the system: regenerated from a draft node, it would implement what none of the node's owners has approved (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug). Waiting, it lets a change to the node be committed before its approval, as a change to any rule is; and since no commit changes it meanwhile, it is still never edited. A copy that waits is left behind its nodes only until every one of them is approved, and its lag is reported meanwhile (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh), so that nobody takes it for current.

children.title: The structure of the specification is defined by its schema
children.text: The structure of every node and every file of the specification is defined by its schema: the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines, with the extension a project's own guidelines add to it. The extension may add only kinds of node (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), fields of an existing kind, which the nodes of the SpecSheriff guidelines need not hold, and properties of a file or of a link, and changes no definition the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds. A file that does not match the schema is refused, and the refusal names the field that is wrong. Why each part of the structure is as it is, is written in the schema beside it.
children.reason:
A structure stated in prose can be broken without anyone noticing; stated as a schema that every file is checked against, it cannot. The schema is therefore the only description of the structure, and a rule that names a part of it, to say what that part means, is compared with it by machine.

A project needs kinds, fields and properties the SpecSheriff guidelines cannot foresee, and they are held as the shared ones are only where they stand in the schema every file is checked against. An extension that changes no definition of the shared schema keeps every structure the SpecSheriff guidelines define the same in every project, so a tool or a reader relying on one is never wrong there.

decisions.problem: The rule named the files the schema is kept in, which is the layout of one toolset rather than what the specification requires.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines apply the split between base and appendix to themselves (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8); where the schema is kept is described in the appendix of the tools.

decisions.problem: The schema every project read was the one the SpecSheriff guidelines carry, and a project's own schema was refused as a copy, so a project's own kinds, fields and properties could not stand.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's own guidelines add an extension to the schema, which may add only kinds of node, fields of an existing kind and properties of a file or of a link, and changes no definition of the shared schema. A field or a property needs no rule of its own, unlike a kind: it exempts nothing, and its values are wording its node's owner confirms.

children.title: A node is one rule, and a section holds rules
children.text: One numbered rule is one node, and its continuation paragraphs, tables and code blocks belong to that node rather than standing beside it. A section is a container of rules: its text states what the section is responsible for and requires nothing, since every requirement is a rule, and it holds at least one rule — a RecordType, a term node or a node of a project's own kind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) counts as one, and the rules of the sections inside it count as its own. A section whose rules have all gone is deleted, and every link and citation naming it is moved to the node that now holds its matter, or removed.
children.reason: A rule's parts only make sense together. Splitting them into nodes of their own would invent a second set of locations for fragments nothing can cite. A requirement written into a section's text is a rule nobody can cite, name in a SpecTag or check on its own, and a section with no rule states a responsibility nothing in the code answers to. A RecordType, a term node and a node of a project's own kind each state on their own what must hold, as a rule does — a RecordType the shape of its data, a term what its word means in every rule that uses it, a node of a project's own kind what its kind is declared for — and each is cited by its sid and named by SpecTags, so a section holding one holds a requirement.

decisions.problem: The check of a checked section counted a data record node and a term node as its rules, while this rule named rules alone, so a section of terms, such as a glossary of contracts, passed the check and broke the rule as written.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record node and a term node count as rules of their section; that terms are not duplicated is held by contracts alone holding them and by no two of them sharing a name.

decisions.problem: A node of a project's own kind did not count as a rule of its section.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: it counts as one.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

children.title: A node is cited by its sid, and its location names where it is in the specification
children.reason: A reference to a place breaks whenever the place changes. A specification that grows is reordered, and its rules move between domains, for as long as it grows. A sid is not a place: moving a node changes its location, never its sid, so no reference holding the sid breaks. The location stays where a person reads, computed so that it can never disagree with where the node is.

decisions.problem: A test in a language whose names cannot hold a hyphen declares its sid by a mark rather than in its name.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a sid is cited in the tests, however a test declares it (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35).

decisions.problem: Only a section and a rule were said to be numbered, while a data record node is numbered too, as its schema says, and a node of a project's own kind is to be.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on the kinds of a project (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2): every node but a term is numbered among those under its parent.

decisions.problem: One thing had two names, the field `id` and the word "address". `id` read as the node's identifier, which is its sid, and "address" was unclear. A record of history was let cite a node by its address in its past lines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: one name, location, for the field and the word; it names where a node is in the specification. Records of history are a project's legacy, not the method's concern, so nothing cites a node by its location, a record of history included.

children.title: What a node's status says
children.reason:
An approved status claims that one of the node's owners agreed to what it now states. A status that survived a rewrite would certify words nobody approved. A draft node asks for no code (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) and tells its owners that it waits for their approval.

A change of owners changes who reads a part, not what a rule states. An owner leaving, or a node moving, takes back nothing that was agreed. Links, metadata and what is built from other nodes are not what an owner approved, and they change as the specification grows around a rule.

A withdrawal gives no agreement in anyone's name: it only makes a node a draft, as a change to its wording by anyone does. So whoever finds an approved rule wrong can keep any further change to its code or its tests from being committed (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) without waiting for its owners. The withdrawal names whoever made it, which tells the owners whom to ask. A project takes the SpecSheriff guidelines as they were approved where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), so their approval is not the project's to withdraw. Whether the rule that approves the specification is approved decides how strictly the checks hold all code and tests, which is the specification's owners' decision (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).

list.of: the values a node's status can take

decisions.problem: A data record node holds its fields apart from its text (s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and a field changed would have left the status standing over a structure the owner never confirmed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record node's fields are part of the wording a confirmation covers.

decisions.problem: A kind of node came to carry values beside its text, and a value changed would have left the status standing over values the owner never confirmed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the values a node's kind carries beside its text are part of the wording a confirmation covers, as a data record node's fields are.

decisions.problem: One person confirmed every node, and the values a confirmation covered were listed by the kinds of node one project uses.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of the part a node stands in confirms it (§s-67vekyup7y8smap), and a confirmation covers whatever values the node's kind carries beside its text. An owner's own change to a wording needs a new confirmation as anyone else's does, since the fingerprint of the wording, not who changed it, decides.

decisions.problem: A move was said to leave the status as it is, while only a node's owner confirms it, so a node moved under another owner stood checked over words that owner never read.
decisions.ruling: The owner: checked means the node's owner confirmed its present wording; a move or a change that gives the node another owner empties its status.

decisions.problem: The reason held that a checked status claims its owner read the words a node holds, while a node may now be confirmed in its owner's name where its change states nothing new.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-67vekyup7y8smap: a checked status claims the owner agreed to what the node states.

decisions.problem: No rule said who may withdraw a confirmation, while the procedure let anyone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: anyone may withdraw a confirmation, and the withdrawal names whoever made it; the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes stay as they were confirmed where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab).

decisions.problem: What is built into a node from other nodes, a domain's header's index of sections, was left out of the wording a confirmation covers by the tools alone, and the values gathered beside a field were to be built so too.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh: a change to what is built into a node from other nodes leaves its status as it is.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: Checked was read three ways once the specification and its domains had a status too: a node's wording confirmed by its owner, every node of a section or a domain confirmed, and a specification put live. A move or a change of owner emptied a node's status, while such a change is most often technical.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node's status is draft or approved, a section's and a domain's header's built from what they hold; whether someone may approve is settled when the approval is given, so a change of owners or a move keeps it.

children.title: The status of a section and of a domain's header
children.text: The status of a section is built from the nodes under it that are no section: approved where every one of them is approved, and draft otherwise. The status of a domain's header is built the same way from every node of the domain but the header itself. Nobody approves a section or a header itself, nor a header's level and where its code is. The status is built anew after every change to the specification and never written by hand.
children.reason: A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg, §s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr): what they state, the nodes under them state, so their own words leave an owner nothing to agree to. A header's level is one of those the project's own guidelines list (§s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4), in a rule the specification's owners approve. Where its code is says where to look, not what must hold. Built from the nodes under it, the status shows at a glance which parts of the specification wait for their owners. Built anew after every change, it never falls behind those nodes (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).

decisions.problem: A section and a domain's header were confirmed as a rule is, so their status claimed an agreement to words that require nothing, and said nothing of the nodes they hold.
decisions.ruling: The owner: their status is the state of what they hold, built and only shown, whatever the number of rules; their own wording is meta-information nobody approves.

children.title: Only its owners approve a node
children.text:
The specification has owners, one or several. A domain (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) or a section may have owners of its own, who take the place of the owners above for every node within it.

A node is approved by one of its owners and by nobody else. An approval names whoever gave it.

An agent working for one of a node's owners approves the node in that owner's name where its wording changes only:

- to state what one of its owners approved in another node;
- by a replacement that changes no meaning, such as a renamed term or path.

The agent reports each such approval to that owner, who may withdraw it.
children.reason:
An approval means that someone who answers for a rule has agreed to what it states, so it is theirs to give. Named, whoever approved is compared with the node's owners and can be asked later. Owners of domains and sections divide the reading as the specification is divided, so that it can grow beyond what one person reads. The owners of one part share its reading, and each of them answers for all of it.

A node whose wording only states what one of its owners approved in another node asks nothing its owners have not agreed to. A replacement that changes no meaning states nothing new. Shown again, either would spend the owners' attention on no decision. An agent working for an owner already acts in that owner's name and reports to them as it works. The report lets the owner see that the change was only that, and withdraw the approval where it was not.

decisions.problem: One owner confirmed every node, which binds a growing specification to one person, and the confirmations were kept outside the specification, where nobody else could check them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a domain may name its owners in its header; a confirmation names who gave it, beside the fingerprint of the wording, is kept with the specification and is accepted only under that owner's signature. A confirmation read off the approvals of a merge request was declined, since it would tie what a status means to one hosting platform.

decisions.problem: Owners could be named on a domain's header alone, and a confirmation was to carry its owner's signature, made with a key no agent can use.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification has one owner, and a domain or a section may have its own, taken as a task is taken, oneself included; a confirmation names its owner and carries no signature, the agent's hooks guarding the status.

decisions.problem: The spec-review skill had the agent confirm, unshown, a node changed only to state what its owner had confirmed in another node, or by a replacement changing no meaning, while this rule let nobody but the owner confirm a node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a node is confirmed in its owner's name by the agent that made the change for that owner, which reports the confirmation to the owner; the owner may withdraw it. The owner amended the principle that nothing unconfirmed is implemented to the same effect.

decisions.problem: A part could name only one owner, while a team shares the reading of a part.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a part may have several owners with equal rights, any of whom approves; the approval names who gave it.

children.title: A draft node is not implemented
children.text: A node is implemented only once it is approved. Before a domain's implementation begins, the domain is reviewed whole; where the implementation then finds a node silent or wrong, that node is changed and reviewed when the problem is found, not later.
children.reason: The specification is expected to be incomplete. Implementing a draft node fills its gap with a guess made in the code, which the specification then does not hold; reviewing the node at once keeps the answer in the specification.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: Removal goes through the archive when an approval was ever given
children.text:
A node an approval was ever given for is moved to the archive when it is removed, together with the reason for its removal and the sid of the node that replaces it, if one does. A section, a domain's header and a node no approval was ever given for are deleted outright, whatever cited them.

A node may later be deleted from the archive.
children.reason:
A rule one of its owners approved is one the code may implement, and a later change to its wording does not undo what was implemented from it, so its removal is worth keeping for a time. Kept in its last wording, it can be restored if its removal is undone. And it is a record for the decisions taken: an approved rule that had to go, a rule of the base above all, most often shows a logic or an approach that was mistaken, which later work has to understand and take into account, as it would a list of the defects found.

Nothing guarantees how long the archive keeps a node, so a link or a citation naming an archived node breaks when the node is deleted, and the checks refuse it until it is removed. A node no approval was ever given for was never implemented, since no SpecTag may name it, and archived it would only bury the rules that had to go under wording nobody approved. A section and a domain's header require nothing and nobody approves them (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs), so no code was implemented from them and their removal keeps nothing worth restoring.

decisions.problem: The reason spoke of the specification's owner, while a confirmation is now given by an owner of the node's part.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of the node's part (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).

decisions.problem: The reason held that the archive keeps resolvable the citations in the code, the tests and the commits that implemented a removed rule, while nothing keeps a node in the archive for good.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the archive keeps a removed node for a time, so that it can be restored and so that later work learns from what was found wrong, as from a list of the defects found; a node may be deleted from it, and a link into it may then break.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A section confirmed under an earlier release would go to the archive when removed, while no section is approved now and an emptied section is deleted (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg).
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-9kfdycuq34beqvs: a section and a domain's header go to no archive.

children.title: A decision lives on the rule it settled
children.text: A decision records what was settled about a rule. It is kept in that rule's metadata, never as a document of its own. A decision usually changes the rule's wording; a procedural one changes none.
children.reason: A decision is not specification but the history of one rule, and it is read beside that rule. The procedural kind would otherwise leave no trace, because nothing in the wording shows it. And the number of decisions on one rule measures how well it was written: a rule that keeps collecting them was written badly.

children.title: Work put off lives on the node it concerns
children.text: Work put off that concerns one node is kept in that node's metadata, as an item of its todos. An item holds the day the work was put off, who its author is and what is to be done. It is never kept in a comment on the node or in a document of its own. A problem of the default implementation set aside is a rule of the technical debt instead (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). An item is removed once it is done or given up. Every item of the todos across the specification can be listed at once, the newest first, each with the node it stands on.
children.reason: Work put off is read beside the node it concerns, as a decision is, so whoever opens the node sees what still waits on it. Its date orders the listing, and its author tells the reader whom to ask. Kept in a comment or a document, it is missed by the listing. An item left once done or given up shows work waiting that no longer waits. Listed together, the items show what waits across the specification. The newest stand first: each older item was weighed at every listing since, a new one at none.

decisions.problem: The schema held a node's todos, but no rule said that work put off is kept there, nor that it can be listed, while a rule is to hold the work deferred on it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: work put off on one node is kept in its todos, with the day, who its author is and what is to be done, and every item can be listed, the newest first, each with its node.

children.title: A rule and its reason are held apart
children.text: A node's text states what must hold, except a rule of the technical debt, which describes a problem as it stands (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). Why it must hold is kept in a separate field of the same node and is not part of the requirement. When a rule is revised, its reason is checked first: a rule whose reason no longer holds is removed, not reworded.
children.reason: Mixed in one text, a rule is long and a reviewer cannot tell which half is being asserted. And a reason that has stopped holding is the surest sign the rule should go — which nobody sees while the reason is buried inside the requirement.

decisions.problem: A rule of the technical debt describes a problem as it stands and states nothing that must hold, which this rule did not admit.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the exception is written here, where the rule it narrows is read.

decisions.problem: The rules call a node's grounds its reason, while the key holding them is rationale, so one thing had two names.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the key becomes reason, renamed with the migration that renames id to location; the key refs stays, a common abbreviation for links that misleads nobody.

children.title: What the specification governs
children.text: The specification describes the system — its logic, its architecture and everything the system is made of — and governs one process only: how the specification itself is kept, changed and implemented. A rule that tries to govern anything else is dropped, and so is a rule that states the obvious.
children.reason: A rule governing what nobody here controls decides nothing: an agent that has never read an instruction cannot be stopped by it, however many are written. Duplication and drift are fought by structure — one model, a generated export, links a checker resolves — not by prohibitions. A rule stating the obvious costs a reading and decides nothing either.

children.title: The specification holds its content; the code implements it
children.text: The specification holds its content and the code implements it, never the reverse. A rule does not hand what it states to a declaration in the code: a set of states, a list of members, a table of routes is described in the specification, and the code is checked against it. A rule that sends its reader to a source file for its content is a defect, repaired when that rule is revised.
children.reason: A specification that leaves a list in the code and names only its meaning cannot say what the system is, and a copy of that list written beside it in prose goes stale with nothing noticing. Held in the specification and checked against the code, the content is in one place and the disagreement is found by a machine.

children.title: A list's member may be an object
children.text: Each member of a list a rule holds is a primitive value or an object. In an object, the property the list names holds the member's value, and the other properties, each a primitive value, a list or an object, hold what is stated of that value.
children.reason: What is stated of a value, held in that value's own object, is never taken for what is stated of another; the named property stays where the value is declared, so the members are read, and compared with their declaration, the same whatever else they hold.

decisions.problem: A project keeps beside each value of a list what it states of that value, as a value's severity, and could write it only as a table in a rule's text, which no tool reads.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a table is held as data; first put as a list's columns, then corrected, since columns are a way of showing data rather than its shape: any member of any list is a primitive value or an object, the property the list names holding the member's value.

children.title: The base specification names no technology
children.text: A rule of the base specification states what the system does, never how the default implementation does it: it names no programming language, library, store, protocol, command or file path. How it is done, and any part of a rule that depends on it, is described in the technical appendix. A technology may be named by example, in brackets, where the rule does not depend on it.
children.reason: The same rules can then be implemented on another stack, with an appendix of its own, without editing a single rule; and a rule that names its tools goes stale when they change, although what the system does has not.

decisions.problem: One rule held what the base names of a technology, of a look and of one instance, and grew too long to read as one requirement.
decisions.ruling: The owner: three rules, one for each.

children.title: Of a user interface the base states what it shows, not how it looks
children.text: Of a user interface, the base specification states what a user can rely on in any instance: what is shown, what it means, in what order, in which states, and what the user can do. How it looks and is built — placement, size, colour, icon, the kind of control, where a state is kept — is described in the technical appendix.
children.reason: The same rules can then be given another look with an appendix of its own; and a rule that names its look goes stale when the look changes, although what the user can rely on has not.

decisions.problem: Nothing said whether the look of a user interface belongs in a rule of the base specification, and rules named column widths, where the browser keeps them and the icons of a menu.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base specification holds what a user can rely on in any instance — what is shown, what it means, its order, its states, what can be done; the technical appendix holds how it looks and is built — placement, sizes, colours, icons, the kind of control, where a state is kept. A menu's order and nesting stay in the base, its icons go to the appendix.

decisions.problem: The rule carried an exception for a menu generated from the specification, which not every project has, and named the person using an interface by one project's term.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project needing such an exception writes it into its own guidelines, refining this rule (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab); the rule speaks of a user.

children.title: The base specification holds no figure of one instance
children.text: The base specification holds no figure measured on an instance — a population, a rate, a duration observed there. A threshold a rule needs is stated by the method an instance measures it with, and its value is a setting of the technical appendix.
children.reason: A figure belongs to the instance it was measured on and to the day it was measured, so every other instance would pass or fail the rule by accident.

decisions.problem: A rule of the writing doctrine forbade numbers measured on a running instance, written to repair rules into which one instance's data had leaked.
decisions.ruling: The owner: in a specification written fresh it is one case of the base being tied to no implementation, and stands beside the rules on technology and on a look.

children.title: The technical appendix stands beside the base specification
children.text:
The technical appendix describes how this repository builds the system — its stack, how each domain is built and how the user interface looks — in the detail an instance needs to repeat it; every part but it and the guidelines is the base specification.

It is no domain and stands at no level, beside the domains as contracts does, with a section for each domain it implements, under that domain's name, one for the stack, and, while any problem is set aside, one for its technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

It never contradicts a rule of the base specification but extends and refines it: a rule too narrow for an implementation is widened in the base, its detail going to the technical appendix.

A node of the appendix describes how the nodes of the base specification it implements are to be carried out, in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and the edge cases of that implementation — and never restates what they state. Each of its nodes but a section, which requires nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg), implements at least one node of the base specification, except a choice covering the whole system, which stands in the section of the stack, and except the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

An instance changes the technical appendix for itself, and what instances vary within it is a setting, described with its default.
children.reason:
The base specification stays stable while an implementation adapts to an instance's infrastructure and requirements, so only the technical appendix changes with an instance.

A part allowed to contradict the base would leave the base binding nowhere, since no rule could be relied on without reading the implementation too. Read beside the nodes it implements, an appendix node restating them would be a second copy, and a copy drifts from what it copies; how a rule is carried out has no other home, since the base names no technology, and described less exactly it would leave a choice to whoever implements it, which the code would then hold and the specification would not.

It is no subject area of the system but the way every one of them is built, which no level can place. A node bound to the rule it implements is found when that rule changes and is read beside it, and divided as the base is, the implementation of a rule is looked for in one place.

The problems set aside are read as one list, so they stand in one section, which spans the domains as the stack does, and a problem is not how a rule is carried out but where carrying it out falls short.

The repository holds nothing of any one instance, so what one instance chooses within the appendix is a setting, not a rule.

decisions.problem: The technical appendix had no stated place beside the domains, nothing said whether it could depart from the base specification, and its nodes were bound to no rule they implement.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the technical appendix stands outside the levels, as contracts does; it never contradicts the base specification but extends and refines it, a rule too narrow being widened in the base; every node implements a node of the base, the choices of the stack excepted; it is divided as the base is; this repository's appendix is the default implementation, an example each instance changes for itself, and it keeps its name, its being the default a detail.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what a node of the technical appendix holds beside the nodes it implements, and a draft retold the base rule it implemented while the values of its implementation had been moved into code.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of the appendix describes how the base nodes it implements are carried out, in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and edge cases — and never restates them, its links carrying what they state; the base answers what is done, the appendix how. Values taken from the code and a running instance while a project's existing documents are brought into the model are a departure recorded in the guide to adopting the method, not in the guidelines.

decisions.problem: The specification had no place for a problem of the implementation the owner set aside, so such a problem waited in the list of tasks as a task nobody meant to do.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the technical appendix holds a technical debt, one list of the problems of the implementation set aside, each only described as it stands; its standing there is the decision to set it aside.

decisions.problem: The rule had each node of the technical appendix implement a node of the base, its sections included, while a section requires nothing and the appendix's sections stand under the names of the domains they implement.
decisions.ruling: Following §s-7445ahgjck2aefg: a section of the technical appendix implements nothing; it stands under the name of the domain it implements.

children.title: The technical debt holds the problems of the default implementation set aside
children.text: The section of the technical debt holds rules alone, each describing one problem of the default implementation as it stands and refining the nodes the default implementation falls short of there, one of the base specification at least; where the problem lies in a technology the default implementation uses, its rule names the version of that technology it was seen in. Standing there is the whole of the decision to set the problem aside: its rule carries no reason, no decision records it, and the change that solves the problem removes the rule.
children.reason: A problem set aside needs a place where it is stated, or it is forgotten, or kept as a task nobody means to do. Every problem there stands for the one reason that the specification's owners judged it not worth solving now, so a reason or a decision of its own would only repeat its standing. Described as it stands and bound to the nodes it concerns, it tells whoever repeats an instance, or reads those nodes, what the implementation does not do; a problem in a technology may be solved by a later version of it while nothing here changes, and the version it was seen in lets a reader tell. Left standing once solved, it would describe a shortfall that no longer exists.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: The guidelines hold their base and the appendix of their tools
children.text: The guidelines are divided as the specification is: their base states what is held, what is checked, when, and what a failure costs, and names no technology; the appendix of the tools describes how one toolset carries that base out — its commands, its hooks, where it keeps the files, how it reads code and who runs its reviewer. Each rule of that appendix implements at least one node of the base. The appendix of the tools is not the technical appendix, which describes how the system is built and never the tools of the specification.
children.reason: The guidelines require of every base specification that it name no technology (§s-5x737t9nee4zgaa) and are held to it themselves: a rule naming its tool goes stale when the tool changes, and another toolset, written in another language, could not implement it. The tools hold the specification and the code to each other rather than make up the system, which is why they are described apart from the technical appendix. Bound to the node of the base it implements, a rule of the appendix is found when that node changes.

decisions.problem: The guidelines named the commands, the hooks, the files and the parser of the tools that check them, which their own rule forbids a base specification to do.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines apply the split between base and appendix to themselves, so that another toolset can implement the same base.

children.title: A project's own guidelines refine or implement the SpecSheriff guidelines
children.text: The guidelines are the SpecSheriff guidelines and a part each project holds as its own: the base of the SpecSheriff guidelines, which every project shares, with the appendix of the toolset the project uses; and the project's own guidelines, which hold what only its specification needs, such as the specification's owners or the list of levels its domains stand at. Each rule of a project's own guidelines refines or implements a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines and never contradicts it. A project holds no copy of the SpecSheriff guidelines: they come whole with the skills that apply them and are updated with them, and are changed only where they are written.
children.reason:
The SpecSheriff guidelines, shared by every project, are what lets a tool, a skill or a reader carry from one project to the next, and a project needs what they cannot foresee. Refining or implementing the SpecSheriff guidelines and never contradicting them, a project's own rules extend them as the technical appendix extends the base, so that a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines can be relied on in every project without reading that project's own.

Coming whole with the skills, the SpecSheriff guidelines read the same in every project working by one release, and stand approved there as they were approved where they are written; a copy changed in one project would be a second version nobody who writes them reads.

decisions.problem: Rules only one project's specification needed stood in the guidelines every project would share.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines hold what every project shares; a project holds what only its specification needs as rules of its own, standing to them as the technical appendix stands to the base.

decisions.problem: The SpecSheriff guidelines were to name owners of their own, as a domain does, so that the confirmations they carried into a project would hold there under signatures that project's owner never gave.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines are no domain and have no owners in a project; a project takes them whole, at a version its specification's owner names, their confirmations stay where they are written, and the checks compare them to that version.

decisions.problem: The part of the guidelines every project takes whole was named the core, a general word that does not say of what.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is named the SpecSheriff guidelines.

decisions.problem: Whether a project names the version of the checks it runs, taking the tools of that version from the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in into a cache on the machine, or the plugin, which Claude Code updates on each machine, carries the tools.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the plugin is a package holding everything its work needs, and every release reaches every machine through the marketplace's update; a machine not yet updated is its user's matter, and a team's CI is its own and left out of the design.

decisions.problem: Whether a project's own guidelines may hold rules tied to no rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines, provided they contradict none.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every rule of a project's own guidelines refines or implements a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines. The link is what lets a reader judge that it contradicts none, which no check can decide, and a rule on keeping the specification that finds no parent there is most likely a rule of the product.

decisions.problem: The rule let a project's own guidelines hold a kind of node of its own, while the schema every project reads admits only the kinds it defines.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-rah8b37kytb682y: the kinds of node are those the schema defines (§s-eferktypcj7njt5), the same in every project.

decisions.problem: The ruling of 2026-10-31 made the kinds of node the same in every project, so a project's own rules needing a kind of their own could not stand.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: a project's own guidelines may declare kinds of node of their own.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/reindex.test.ts::@spec s-bsya3febm6u64ab leaves the status of the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes as it stands, and judges it where they are written

children.title: A project's own kind of node is numbered, counted and implemented as a rule is
children.text:
The nodes of a project's own kind, declared in the extension of the schema (§s-eferktypcj7njt5), are numbered as rules are (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx) and count as rules of the section they stand in (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg). Unless the extension declares that they need no code, which exempts them from being implemented (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf), they are implemented and tested as a rule is (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf, §s-rah8b37kytb682y).

A rule of the project's own guidelines, refining this one, lists each such kind with whether its nodes need code, and the list names the extension as its declaration, against which the check of lists compares it (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).
children.reason: A project needs kinds of node the SpecSheriff guidelines cannot foresee, and most are one more kind of requirement, so a kind is held as a rule is unless declared otherwise, and no check meets a node whose duties nobody stated. A kind whose nodes need no code is exempted once, for all its nodes; listed in a rule of the project's own guidelines, it is approved by one of the specification's owners, as every exemption is (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf).

decisions.problem: A project's own rules needed kinds of node the schema did not admit, and the rulings of 2026-10-31 had made the kinds of node the same in every project.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project declares kinds of its own in the extension of the schema, each held as a rule is unless its nodes need no code. Whether a test is owed belongs to the code, written or generated, not to the kind, so the kind needs no more; no kind of container, since a section, to which the extension may add fields, groups nodes; each kind listed in a rule of the project's own guidelines, which its owner confirms.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/binding.test.ts::@spec s-vsh384ybt4w25a2 reports an approved node of a project's own kind that needs code and has none, but not one that needs no code, and lets a test carry its sid
skills/tools/test/unit/model.test.ts::@spec s-vsh384ybt4w25a2 numbers the nodes of a project's own kind among the rules of their section
skills/tools/test/unit/validate.test.ts::@spec s-vsh384ybt4w25a2 counts a node of a project's own kind as a rule of its section, and lets an exempts link reach it

children.title: Data structures are described in the specification
children.text:
A structure of data the domains pass to one another or keep in a store is described by a node of its own, a RecordType: its name, what it is, each of its fields with its type in neutral terms, any bounds on the field's value included, whether the field is required and what it says, what happens to a field nobody declared, and, where another RecordType refers to it by an identifier, the field that identifies it. The rules that bind one field to another are rules linked to the RecordType.

The implementation's types and its checks of data at runtime are generated from the RecordTypes and never written beside them; which mechanism performs the checks is described in the technical appendix.
children.reason: Written beside the description, a type or a check is a second copy of the same structure and drifts from it; generated, the two cannot disagree. A structure is part of what the system is, so it belongs in the specification rather than in the code. The bounds a value may take are part of its type. An identifier of a record has the type of the field that identifies it, so that field is named where its RecordType is described.

decisions.problem: A data record node could not say which values a number field may take, so the bounds of a setting were stated by no node while two components each checked them by hand.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the bounds go into the field's type, named as JSON Schema names them, and the check is generated from them, over writing them in the field's words or dropping them.

decisions.problem: The rule had every value choosing a form be a form, so a value carrying nothing got a form holding nothing, and it did not say when a field is required, so values that may not come were required; worded in one long rule, it was hard to read.
decisions.ruling: The owner: base data, set beforehand or made by the system, is required; additional data is required where its case guarantees it and optional otherwise; a form exists only where a value carries fields of its own. The rule is divided: this one keeps what a data record node holds and that types are generated from it, and three rules of their own say when a field is required, when a value has a form, and where each value choosing a form is declared.

decisions.problem: No node could hold a data record's structure, and a data record whose body differs with its kind had no way to be described at all.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record is described by a node of its own, with its fields; a data record whose fields depend on its kind holds the fields common to every kind and those its kind brings.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what type an identifier of a data record has, and nothing named the field that identifies a data record.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an identifier has the type of the field that identifies the data record it names, which that data record's node names.

decisions.problem: A data record node could not say that a field of type list of always holds at least one member, so the bound would have been stated only in words and its check written by hand beside the data record.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a field's type carries every bound on the field's value, a list's on how many members it holds among them, and this rule names no type, so that which type takes which bound is said where the types are listed.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: A field is required only where its value is guaranteed
children.text: A field is required where every record that can hold it has its value: the value is set before the record is written, the system makes or observes it whenever it writes the record, or the system refuses to write the record without it, as what identifies the record. Every other field is optional: one whose value only some records, or some moments of a record, have, or one an answer the system reads may not carry.
children.reason: A value that may not come cannot be demanded: demanded, it is invented to fill the field, or a record that should have been written is refused for want of it.

decisions.problem: Nothing said when a field of a data record is required, so values that may not come were declared required, and a value carrying nothing was given a form holding nothing.
decisions.ruling: The owner: formal fields, set beforehand or made by the system, are required; additional fields are required where their case guarantees them, as an identifier an external system gives a data record that cannot exist without it, and optional otherwise, as an external system's answer.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: A RecordType variant exists only for a value carrying fields of its own
children.text: Where a RecordType's fields depend on the values of some of its own fields, the RecordType names those fields as choosing its variant. A value that brings fields of its own has a RecordType variant: a RecordType in the part of the specification declaring that value (§s-xfwuvd3funutmsw), which refines the RecordType, names the values it answers to and declares those fields. A value that brings none has no variant, and a record holding it holds only its RecordType's own fields.
children.reason: A variant holding nothing says nothing the declaration of its value does not, so it would be a second copy of that declaration. A variant is held by the part of the specification declaring its value, so that part adds a variant without changing the RecordType or the variants another part holds.

decisions.problem: Every value choosing a data record's form had a form, so a value carrying nothing got a form holding nothing; and form, a general word, named both a data record's shape and what a user fills in on a page.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a value carrying no field of its own has no form, which was a crutch; and the data record's form is named data record variant, a form staying what a user fills in.

decisions.problem: Nothing limited a data record to one field of type variant, and with two it is left unsaid which of them holds the fields of the chosen variant.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record holds at most one field of type variant, which its schema checks. Fields that do not depend on the variant are the data record's own, or the fields its field of type variant holds whatever the variant; two independent choices are two data records, each choosing its own variant.

decisions.problem: A data record in contracts may name fields choosing its variant, and a value its field's own list declares is then declared in contracts, which is not a domain, so no variant could stand where this rule placed it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a variant stands in the part of the specification declaring its value, a domain or contracts, as the tools already held it.

decisions.problem: The part declaring a value was named as a domain or contracts, while a value now comes from a domain, a domain's list or a node.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-xfwuvd3funutmsw: the part declaring a value is the one that rule names.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: One source for the values of a field of type one of
children.text: The values of a field of type one of come from exactly one of the sources this rule lists, and each value is declared once.
children.reason: Coming from one source, a field's values are found whole where its declaration points — by its reader, by the type generated for it (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9) and by the check comparing each variant with the values it names (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j) — while values coming from two would be read from one of them as if it held them all. A value declared twice could be removed in one place while it stays in the other.

decisions.problem: The values choosing a data record's variant were read off its variants alone, so a value without one had to be given a variant holding nothing, and values declared in a sentence no tool can read were checked against no variant.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each value is declared once, in a place a tool reads, whether or not a variant answers to it.

decisions.problem: The rule bound only a field choosing a data record variant, to two places of its values, while a project's fields take their values from the domains, from another field and from the nodes of a kind; and it held in one node the places, how a domain's list names its field and where a value is declared.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the values of a field of type one of come from exactly one source, each value declared once; the sources are listed here, held as a list so the schema's declaration of them is checked against it, and each is described by a rule refining this one, every node holding one thought. A value with no variant needs no clause here, since §s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j gives it none. A field takes nothing by itself, the owner holding that it contains the values its source gives, and a title names the node's matter rather than repeating its text.

decisions.problem: The sources listed let a field's values be those of another field, so that a set two fields share is declared once.
decisions.ruling: The owner: no field's values are another field's, since the lists of two fields would then cross and tie the fields together; each list stands on its own.

list.of: the sources the values of a field of type one of come from
members: the sids of a kind's nodes

children.title: The list of a field's values in contracts may consolidate values from different domains
children.text: Only a field of type one of in a RecordType described in contracts may have as its values those the domains add, each domain listing the values it adds in a rule of its own.
children.reason: A RecordType described in contracts is shared by the domains, and so are its fields, so each domain may add the values it brings, and the variants answering to them (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j), without changing the RecordType, which the owners of contracts hold. A RecordType one domain provides is described in that domain (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), so that domain alone answers for its fields' values and declares them itself.

decisions.problem: The rule named, beside a field's own list of values, the tables one project's tools read such values from.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines keep the field's own list, and a project's own guidelines may declare such values elsewhere (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab).

decisions.problem: The rule allowed a place a project's own guidelines name for a variant's values, and nothing described how they name it, so the tools read the field's own list alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the other place stays and is described. For a data record described in contracts, a rule of a domain defines a list of the field's values and refines the data record by its sid; the tools collect the values from every such list and refuse one declared twice, the variant stands where its value is declared, and the generated types list every value. A data record one domain provides keeps its values in its own field, as the rule on contracts requires.

decisions.problem: The values the domains add to a field of contracts stood in one rule with every other source of a field's values, named the lists of domains, which read as the list of the domains, and stated from the field's side.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the list of a field's values declared in contracts may consolidate values from different domains, the field being shared by them; only such a field may have as its values those the domains add, each domain listing its own in a rule of its own, and a data record one domain provides declares its fields' values itself.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: How a domain's added values find their field
children.text: A domain's rule that adds values to a field of a RecordType in contracts refines that RecordType, and its list names the field the values go to.
children.reason: A RecordType may have several fields of type one of, so the list names the field its values go to; the rule is linked to the RecordType by its sid, so the link holds when the RecordType is renamed.

decisions.problem: How a domain's rule adding values names the field they go to stood in one rule with every source of a field's values, and was then put so that the owner could not tell which values and which field were meant.
decisions.ruling: The owner: held in a rule of its own, put plainly: the rule refines the field's data record, and its list names the field the values go to.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: Domain names as a field's values
children.text: The values of a field of type one of may be the names of the domains, read from the specification: a domain added or removed adds or removes a value.
children.reason: The names of the domains are already held by the specification, so a field whose values they are declares none of them again and cannot fall behind it.

decisions.problem: A project's field naming a domain declared the domains' names in a list of its own, kept by hand beside the domains.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a domain is an entity of the method, so the list of the domains is read from the specification itself, a domain added or removed adding or removing a value.

children.title: Sids of a kind's nodes as a field's values
children.text: The values of a field of type one of may be the sids of the nodes of one kind standing in the base specification, read from the specification: a node of that kind added or archived adds or removes a value.
children.reason: The sids of a kind's nodes are already held by the specification, so a field whose values they are declares none of them again and cannot fall behind it. They are read from the base specification alone: an instance changes the technical appendix for itself (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v), so a value read from it would differ from one instance to the next, and the guidelines describe no system, so a value read from them would name nothing of it.

decisions.problem: A project's field naming a node of a kind of its own, as a step of a job, declared the nodes' sids again in a list kept by hand beside them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: SpecSheriff knows nothing of a project's own things and gives a general source a project points at them, the sids of the nodes of one kind; read from the base specification alone, so that the values are the same in every instance and a variant answering to one stands where data records are described.

children.title: Where a value is declared
children.text: A value of a field of type one of is declared in the part of the specification where the list, the domain or the node it comes from stands.
children.reason: Whoever answers for a list, a domain or a node then declares the values coming from it, and adds the variant answering to each (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j), without changing another part.

decisions.problem: A data record variant stands in the part declaring its value, and only a domain or contracts were named as that part, while a value now comes from a domain, a domain's list or a node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a value is declared in the part where the list, the domain or the node it comes from stands.

children.title: Gathered values stand beside their field
children.text: Where the values of a field of type one of are gathered from elsewhere in the specification, all of them are written beside the field, each with the node it comes from. They are gathered anew after every change to the specification and never written by hand.
children.reason: Beside the field, its values are read whole where the field is described, without searching the parts they come from (§s-k73czmpkazcx7mu), and the node each comes from tells whom to ask about it. Gathered anew after every change, they never fall behind their source, as a list kept by hand would (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).

decisions.problem: The values gathered for a field from the domains were held only in memory, by the checks and the generated types, so a reader of the field saw none of them where it is described.
decisions.ruling: The owner: what a procedure gathers is written into one place at once, the procedure giving the current list at every run; the values a field gathers from elsewhere in the specification are written beside the field, each with the node it comes from, gathered anew after every change, never written by hand, and no part of the wording a confirmation covers, so a domain adding a value leaves a data record of contracts checked.

children.title: What the domains share is agreed in contracts
children.text: Contracts is not a domain: it belongs to none of them and agrees what they share and how they work together — the terminology, the conventions every domain's API follows, and the rules that bind more than one domain. A domain coins no term of its own — a term it needs is added to contracts — and a term is defined once: one term naming two things, or two terms naming one, is refused. What only one domain needs, it holds itself. A RecordType one domain provides to others is described in that domain, as part of its interface; contracts describes a RecordType only where no single domain provides it, as a store more than one domain writes.
children.reason: Domains that coin their own words, or their own conventions for the same exchange, stop understanding one another, and a reader cannot tell whether two words mean one thing. Holding in contracts only what binds more than one domain keeps it from owning what a single domain defines. A RecordType described away from the domain that provides it has no owner: the provider changes what it gives while its description stands elsewhere.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: The division of the specification
children.text: The base specification is made of contracts and of one domain or several. A domain is the part of the base specification devoted to one subject area of the system, and no other domain is responsible for that area.
children.reason: A subject area's rules bear on one another and change together, so they are kept together and apart from those of other areas. A domain describes the RecordTypes it provides to the others as its interface (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), and its header's consumes links name the sections of theirs it uses (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7), so that a change to a domain's rules, outside its interface and the sections others use, leaves the other domains as they are. A system of one such area has no line to divide it along.

decisions.problem: The rule had no reason, and its first sentence read as though every specification were divided into several domains, while a system of one subject area is one domain.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base specification is contracts and one domain or several, the rules on domains holding wherever it is divided; the reason gives the grounds of the division — the rules of one area kept together, and a domain decoupled from the others by the data records it provides as its interface and the sections of theirs it uses — while a link of any type still crosses a domain line.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: A part of the specification can be read alone
children.text: Each domain, contracts, the technical appendix and the guidelines are held apart, and a part too large to read at once is divided into one file per section.
children.reason: The specification is too large to fit whole into the context window of an agent working with it. It is therefore divided into self-contained domains, and a domain into sections, so that only the part the work at hand needs is loaded. Contracts is the exception: shared by every domain, it is loaded whichever part the work needs.

children.title: An entity is declared once
children.text: Every entity of the system — what a term names, such as a user or a session — is declared once: by the term that names it, in contracts (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), and its data, where the specification describes them, by one RecordType, standing in the domain that provides it or, where no single domain does, in contracts. No two RecordTypes share a name.
children.reason: Two definitions of one entity are two owners of it, and two owners change it apart; the duplicate is usually the first visible trace of one domain doing another's work.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: A domain's specification opens with its header
children.text: A domain's specification opens with its header: a node stating what the domain does, its owners where it names them (§s-67vekyup7y8smap), the level it stands at and where its code is, whose consumes links name the sections of other domains the domain uses. The header also carries the index of the domain's sections — each one's sid, title and text, the text of a section stating what that section is responsible for, and the domains that use it — built from the sections and never written by hand.
children.reason: Whoever works on one domain loads its header and learns from it alone what the domain is responsible for, who answers for its wording, how it is divided and what it takes from the others, without loading the rest. The index is built rather than written, because a table of contents kept by hand is a second copy of the sections and drifts from them.

decisions.problem: The owners of a domain had nowhere to be named.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the header names them (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).

decisions.problem: Whether a domain may leave its header out, and whether a section has a header of its own, as a node of service carrying its metadata.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every domain opens with its header, which alone gives it its level, and so its place on the map and in the order of the domains; a section has none, since its own text says what it is responsible for and it names its own owner.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/reindex.test.ts::@spec s-yggv9myedprnaa7 names in a header's index the headers of the domains using a section
skills/tools/test/unit/reindex.test.ts::@spec s-yggv9myedprnaa7 rebuilds the index in a domain's header from the domain's sections

children.title: A domain uses another domain's RecordTypes only from the sections it declares
children.text: A RecordType of one domain names a RecordType of another domain, in a field's type or as the RecordType it refines, only where the named RecordType stands in a section the first domain's header names in its consumes links. A RecordType named from elsewhere is reported, not refused.
children.reason: A domain's header then names every section of another domain whose RecordTypes the domain relies on at runtime, and that domain's index names it beside each one, so whoever changes such a RecordType sees which domains it reaches (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7). A RecordType of contracts is provided by no single domain (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), so naming it makes a domain rely on no other. A RecordType named from elsewhere is reported rather than refused, since declaring the use may set the domains using one another in a cycle (§s-uw9n84edf7cbe9n), which only a change to the design removes; until then the work goes on with the dependency in view.

decisions.problem: A data record of one domain could name one of another that its header's consumes links did not name, so the domain relied on the other at runtime with no header showing it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the domains are decoupled by data at runtime, the data records a domain provides being its interface; the check is kept and warns rather than refuses, and a link of any type still crosses a domain line (§s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws).

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: Every domain stands at a level
children.text: Every domain stands at one of the levels the specification's owners list in the project's own guidelines (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), from the general to the particular: the smaller a domain's responsibility, the lower its level. A level is always shown as its number and its name together, and its number is its place in that list.
children.reason: The links between domains give an order but not a place: a domain that uses nothing may be where the others start or stand apart from them, and one that nothing uses may be where they end or stand over them. The level says which.

decisions.problem: The rule listed the levels one project's domains stand at, which another project's domains need not.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines keep that every domain stands at a level, from the general to the particular; the list of levels is the project's, in its own guidelines (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab).

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: The order of the domains
children.text: The domains are ordered by the consumes links of their headers: a domain stands after every domain it uses and as close as possible before the domains that use it; where the links put two domains in the same place, they stand in the order of their names. The domains do not use one another in a cycle.
children.reason: A domain cannot work without the domains it uses, so this is the order the domains are specified and built in, and computed from the links it cannot disagree with them. Standing as close as possible before its users, a domain is taken up when the first of them needs it. A cycle has no such order.

decisions.problem: The reason rested the refusal of a cycle on a rule outside the guidelines, which a project need not hold.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason stands on the order alone, which a cycle cannot have.

decisions.problem: Whether domains using one another in a cycle should be refused or only reported, since domains link to one another across their lines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the cycle stays refused. It is read from the consumes links of the domains' headers alone, not from the links between their rules, which may cross domain lines freely; a cycle of consumes leaves no order to specify and build the domains in, and usually shows a part both share that belongs in contracts or in a domain below them.

decisions.problem: The section was titled "The model", which said neither what it holds nor that its rules are not the specification itself but those it is kept by.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the section is titled "The foundations": it holds the rules every other section rests on, what the specification is made of and how it is changed. A title naming the approach was weighed and set aside as longer than needed.

children.title: Links
children.text: How one node of the specification bears on another.

children.title: Outgoing links are written, incoming links are built
children.text:
A node declares the links it makes, each naming the node it points at, and, for every other node it cites — `§` followed by that node's sid, in any of its fields but its links, the nodes under it, a header's index of its sections and the values gathered beside a field, text quoted as code included — at least one naming that node.

The links pointing at it stand in the same list, each naming the node it comes from and read from this node's end; they are rebuilt from those declarations — every such entry removed first and built again — and are never written by hand.

A node of the archive is held to neither: it holds no link pointing at it, and none it declares is built into another node.

A node of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds only the links pointing at it from the SpecSheriff guidelines.
children.reason:
A reverse link kept by hand survives the removal of its other end and then reads as a live relation. Rebuilt from scratch every time, the reverse direction is correct whatever was skipped before. Held in one list with the links the node makes, they show every relation of the node from where it stands, the end each entry names telling the direction.

A citation relies on the node it names as a link does; with no link of its own it is seen only where it is written, and missed by whoever changes the node it names. Quoted as code, as in a diagram drawn there, a citation relies on the node it names all the same. A header's index and the values gathered beside a field copy what other nodes hold, and the links stay with those nodes.

A node of the archive is no longer part of the specification, and a link built to or from it would read as a live relation.

The SpecSheriff guidelines read the same in every project working by one release (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), and a list in them of the links one project makes to them would hold true of that project alone.

decisions.problem: A citation in a node was only a candidate for a link whose type a review was to name, a step no rule stated and nobody took, until hundreds of citations named nodes their own node held no link to, and the nodes cited showed nobody citing them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: no candidates — a node citing another declares the link to it, of the type that says how the two bear on each other or cites, and the reindex builds the side pointing at the node cited as it does for every link; a citation with no link is refused, and the links the citations lacked are written once.

decisions.problem: A project's own guidelines refine or implement rules of the SpecSheriff guidelines, which a project reads from the plugin for Claude Code and never writes, so the links pointing at those rules could not be held there; and where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written, the links its own project guidelines make would have been written into them and carried to every project.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's links to the SpecSheriff guidelines are one-way, as a law lists no act made under it; links in both directions stay everywhere else, between the rules of a project's specification and the nodes implementing them.

decisions.problem: The links pointing at a node are built from the links the nodes make, so they could be computed whenever they are asked for rather than stored in the node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: they stay stored in the node, so that an agent opening a node sees what depends on it without remembering to ask.

decisions.problem: A citation quoted as code was not read, so a diagram drawn in a code block, citing the nodes of each step, held no links to them; and the values gathered beside a field name nodes as a header's index does.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node mentioned is a node linked, so `§` followed by a real sid is a citation everywhere in a node, text quoted as code included; a form of the notation with no sid after `§` cites nothing. The values gathered beside a field are left out as a header's index is, since the links stay with the nodes they copy.
