children.title: A link carries its type
children.text:
Every link names what it means, as one of these types: implements — the linking node is how the linked one is carried out; refines — it states the linked node more precisely, or for a narrower case; constrains — it holds a condition the linked rule depends on; consumes — the domain whose header holds the link uses what the linked section of another domain provides; supersedes — it replaces the linked node, which is archived; exempts — a node of the project's own guidelines takes the linked rule or node of a project's own kind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), or every such node under the linked section, out of the rule that it is implemented (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf), for the reason its text gives; cites — the linking node cites the linked one (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz) and no other type says how the two bear on each other, so it holds no link of another type to it; term-relation — the linking term and the linked term are bound, for as long as both exist, in the ratio the link carries; uses — what the linking term names makes use of what the linked term names while taking part in a process, as a user fills in a form while signing up, and the link carries no ratio; a term that only starts a process, as an operator starting an export, uses nothing the process uses.

A term-relation and a uses link bind two terms, and no other type does, cites included: a term citing another term holds a term-relation or a uses link to it.

A ratio is the multiplicity of each end in the usual notation, 1, 0..1, 1..N or 0..N, the linking term's end first — user 1:0..N session says that a user has any number of sessions and that a session belongs to exactly one user. Read from the linked term, the ratio is reversed.
children.reason:
A link without a type records only that somebody thought of two nodes together: no check can grade it and no diagram can draw it. A type named without its meaning is the same guess one step later.

A citation is typed by the words around it where no name of a type says more, so its link has a type of its own rather than none. A use is kept apart from a term-relation because making use of something does not last and has no number to it: given a ratio, it states a multiplicity nobody means. A term that only starts a process takes no part in it, so a use of what the process uses would claim a part it never takes.

An exemption is a link rather than a mark on the exempted rule, so that one node gives the reason for every rule it exempts, and each exempted rule outside the SpecSheriff guidelines shows, among its incoming links, what exempts it.

list.of: the types a link between nodes of the specification can carry

decisions.problem: A person fills in a form another term builds, and no ratio fitted that relation: it lasts only while the form is filled, and a term-relation states a multiplicity that holds for as long as both terms exist.
decisions.ruling: A second type of link between terms, uses, carrying no ratio; a term-relation is bound for as long as both terms exist.

decisions.problem: A person only starting a process was nearly linked to what that process uses, as if taking part in it.
decisions.ruling: A uses link is for a term taking part in a process; one that only starts it uses nothing the process uses.

decisions.problem: A form of a data record refines the data record (s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and refines was defined over rules alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: one word changes, rule to node — a form of a data record is the data record for a narrower case; a longer definition was declined as padding.

decisions.problem: A link declared for a citation had no type to take where none of the types said how the two nodes bear on each other, which left the citation a candidate for a link nobody typed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a link has a type of its own, cites, standing only where no other type describes the two nodes.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: No type of link could take a rule out of the rule that a checked rule is implemented.
decisions.ruling: The owner: exempts, from a node of a project's own guidelines to a rule or a section.

decisions.problem: An exempts link could take only a rule out of being implemented.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: it takes a node of a project's own kind as well.

children.title: A link may cross a domain line
children.text: A link between nodes of the specification may cross a domain line: a rule of one domain may point at a rule of another, and the link carries its type like any other. Whoever would point at a statement of another domain that no node there holds first gives it to a node of that domain that can carry it, or, failing one, writes a rule there whose todos name the node linking to it, and links to that node.
children.reason: Domains build on one another — a later one uses what an earlier one provides — and the specification has to be able to say so. A link holds the sid of the node it points at, so moving either node leaves it whole, and a link to a node that no longer exists is refused by the checker the same day. A statement named in words rather than by a node is a reference no check can follow, and the node it means shows nobody relying on it; given to a node there it keeps one home, and a rule written for a link is read when its domain is, its todo saying why it stands there.

decisions.problem: The citation check refused a citation crossing a domain line unless it named a node of a few domains, a list the tool kept and no rule stated, and such citations had been replaced by the words of the rule they named; that a citation into another domain names a node there stood nowhere.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a link of any type, cites among them, crosses a domain line freely and is checked only for naming a node, over admitting one only into what the linking domain's header consumes; a statement no node of the other domain holds is given to a node there, or a rule is written there for the link.

children.title: Code
children.text: How the code implements the specification and the tests verify it.

children.title: The system's code is the code implementing the specification, and its tests
children.text: The system's code is the code implementing the specification outside its guidelines, written by hand or generated from its nodes, and the tests verifying that code. The repository's configuration, its own tools and the tests of those tools are not the system's code. A project's own checks and generators are among those tools (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze). The two are told apart by where each lives.
children.reason: Code and its tests are written together, the test first (§s-rah8b37kytb682y). A rule counts as implemented only by a symbol carrying its SpecTag together with a passing test carrying its SpecTag (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf), so the tests belong with the code they verify. Code generated from a node is part of the system as much as code written by hand. The repository's configuration and its own tools serve the work on the system, not what the system does. Where a file lives reads the same to every check, so it decides on which side the file is.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what the system's code is, while the base names it throughout, and the repository's tools, its configuration and every test were exempt from tags by where they live.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the system's code is the code implementing the specification, its tests included, since they are written first; the repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are not.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The node named a test's reference to its node a sid, or read a SpecTag as standing only on a symbol, once a test came to carry a SpecTag too.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's rulings of that day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: the test's reference is its SpecTag, and what binds the symbols reads those outside the tests.

children.title: Code changes only as a consequence of the specification
children.text: Behaviour changes by changing the specification first; the change to the code follows from it. Every commit that changes code names, by its sid, each approved node whose implementation it adds or changes — one whose text has just changed, or an existing one the code contradicted — and, outside the tests, every SpecTag on a symbol it adds or changes names a node the message names, or is the SpecTag that names none. The message names no domain's header and no section.
children.reason: Wanting different behaviour is a reason to change the specification, not the code. A commit that repairs code which contradicted the specification as it stood is the same procedure and not an exception to it: there the specification was already right. The message and the SpecTags on the code name the same nodes so that the message says which nodes the commit serves, and a header or a section is refused because it requires nothing a change could serve.

decisions.problem: A commit changing a domain's code named the domain's header, which says nothing of what the commit changed, and the check of the message accepted it, since any node that exists was accepted.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code changes only through the specification. A commit names the checked rules it serves, the tags of the declarations it changes name those rules, and a header or a section never stands in for a rule.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The node named a test's reference to its node a sid, or read a SpecTag as standing only on a symbol, once a test came to carry a SpecTag too.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's rulings of that day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: the test's reference is its SpecTag, and what binds the symbols reads those outside the tests.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: Three records, each answering a different question
children.reason:
Each answers a different question. The SpecTag on a symbol says what the symbol implements. The SpecTag a test declares says which rule the test is written from. Reported by a run of the tests, it makes the run itself a report of which rules are covered. The lists say what implements a rule, to a reader who has the rule open.

The SpecTag on a symbol and the one a test declares take one form, since each binds the code or the test to a node by its sid. A reference in that form is told apart from a sid that is only mentioned.

decisions.problem: A test bound to its rule by the opening of its name cannot be written in a language whose names cannot hold a hyphen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test declares the sid of what it verifies however its language allows, so that a run of the tests reports it.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A symbol named its node by a SpecTag while a test opened its name with the bare sid or held it in a mark: two forms of one reference.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test declares its node by a SpecTag too, standing where the bare sid stood, so that every binding of code or a test to a node takes one form and a run of the tests still shows it.

skills/tools/test/unit/binding.test.ts::@spec s-rwqzepmrt77rv35 refuses a node's lists of code and tests that the tags and the tests' sids do not produce

children.title: The test comes before the code
children.text:
When a rule is implemented, its test is written first and the code that implements it second, written to pass that test. The test carries the rule's SpecTag (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35), and so does the code that implements it (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4).

Every test carries the SpecTag of the rule, the term or the node of a project's own kind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) it is written from. A test a commit adds or changes carries the SpecTag of an approved one. Every rule, or node of a project's own kind that needs code, whose code written for it a commit adds or changes has at least one test. Code generated from a node owes none.

Rewriting a test's reference to its node into another form that names the same node changes no test.
children.reason:
A test names a rule's behaviour, which survives the refactoring that moves and renames the code underneath it, so the binding through tests is the stable one. And a test written first tests the rule, not whatever the code happened to do.

A term whose definition states behaviour is verified as a rule is, and its test carries the term's own SpecTag rather than that of a rule written only to repeat it. A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr). Code generated from a node, as the types and runtime checks of a RecordType are (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), is held by every commit to what the node produces (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j), so a test of its own would verify the generator rather than the system's code.

A test without the SpecTag of the node it is written from tests something nobody can name, and a rule whose code has no test is carried out on trust; both are refused where the change is made, which is when a test costs least to write. Only a test a commit adds or changes must name an approved node, since a rule under revision is a draft while the tests written against its earlier wording still stand.

A reference rewritten into another form names the same node, so the test is held to nothing new. Counted as a change, it would refuse, at the commit rewriting it, every test whose node is under revision.

children.title: Every symbol carries a SpecTag, and what carries no rule says so
children.text:
Every symbol of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) outside its tests — a function, a class or a member of one, a type, a constant, a component — carries a SpecTag naming the node it implements. This holds wherever in the code the symbol stands and whichever domain the node belongs to. A symbol inside another is covered by the SpecTag of the one it stands in.

Some symbols implement none of the system's logic but are required by the technology the system is built with. Such a symbol carries instead a SpecTag that names no node and gives its reason. Examples are a module's re-exports and the glue a framework, a library or the infrastructure needs.

Only a symbol whose code a commit changes must name an approved node. A change to its SpecTags is a change to its code. Rewording the rest of its comments, moving a citation onto another sid or renaming an identifier everywhere it is spelled changes no code.
children.reason:
A SpecTag on every symbol is what makes logic without a rule visible. A symbol left without a SpecTag until somebody changes it hides until then whether any rule asks for it. One SpecTag per file lets every symbol added to it later go untraced. A binding read by the domain a file stands in misses code that implements another domain's rule.

Code that serves the technology the system is built with exists because of how the system is built, not because of what it does, so there is no rule for it to cite. Demanding one teaches people to attach whichever sid is nearest. Marking it explicitly keeps 'nobody gave it a SpecTag' apart from 'there is nothing for a SpecTag to name'.

Only a symbol whose code changes must name an approved node, since a rule under revision is a draft while the code written against its earlier wording still stands. A comment reworded, a citation moved or a name changed everywhere it is spelled changes nothing the code does. A SpecTag counts as code because it decides which node the code is held to. Were a change to it not counted, a SpecTag could be moved onto a draft node, or onto one the code does not implement, with nothing refusing it.

decisions.problem: One tag per changed file was owed, and only in a domain with a checked rule of its own, so code implementing two checked rules of another domain shipped with no tag, and logic no rule stated passed beside it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code changes only through the specification and never the reverse, enforced by scripts that refuse logic without a reference back to the specification and by an independent reviewer; every declaration a commit adds or changes carries a tag, in every domain and in contracts.

decisions.problem: A tag was owed only by a declaration a commit added or changed, so code nobody had touched since the rules were written stayed untagged, and whether a rule asked for it could not be seen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every declaration always carries a tag; a project adopting the method tags its code before the check is turned on.

decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2: the check refuses every untagged symbol from the commit putting the specification live.

decisions.ruling: The owner: every symbol of the system's code but its tests carries a tag; a test carries the sid of the node it is written from, since it is written from the node's logic and verifies the code written for it.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's rulings of that day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: the test's reference is its SpecTag, and what binds the symbols reads those outside the tests.

decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: An approved rule is implemented or exempted
children.text:
Every approved rule, and every approved node of a project's own kind that needs code (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), is implemented: a symbol of the system's code carries its SpecTag, and a test carries its SpecTag and passes. A SpecTag or a test naming a rule that implements it, directly or through rules that implement those in turn, counts for it.

This holds for every rule of the specification but those of the SpecSheriff guidelines, of the project's own guidelines and of the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

A node of the project's own guidelines exempts a rule, or a node of a project's own kind, from being implemented through an exempts link to it, or to a section it stands under (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm), and gives the reason in its own text.
children.reason:
An approved rule states what holds of the system it specifies, what the system does or how it is built, so one the system's code does not carry out leaves the specification stating what does not hold of it. A SpecTag shows where the code carries the rule out (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), and a test naming the rule shows that the code does what the rule says, but only while it passes, as every test of the system's code must at a push while the specification is approved (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh); only both together show it by a check. A SpecTag or a test of a rule implementing it counts, since an implementing rule is how the rule it implements is carried out (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm).

The SpecSheriff guidelines are carried out by the tools and the skills that apply them, never by code a SpecTag binds: a project does not hold that code, and the repository writing them keeps it out of the system's code by where it lives (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc). A project's own guidelines, which hold what only its specification needs (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), are carried out by those tools and skills and by people, not by the system's code; and a rule of the technical debt describes a problem set aside, which is not required of the system and goes once it is solved (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). A rule the system's code cannot carry out, or that no test can verify, would be reported for as long as it stands, so it is exempted; the exemption is a node, which one of its owners approves with its reason.

decisions.problem: Nothing reported a checked rule that the system's code did not carry out: a test was required only once a commit changed a rule's code, so a rule nobody reached stood unnoticed while the specification stated it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every checked rule is implemented — a symbol of the system's code tagged with it and a passing test carrying its sid, a tag or a test of a rule implementing it counting — or is exempted by a node of the project's own guidelines with an exempts link; the SpecSheriff guidelines, the project's own guidelines and the technical debt are outside it, where the guidelines are written as well.

decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: it is implemented as a rule is, unless its kind needs no code, and is exempted as a rule is.

decisions.problem: The system's code came to include its tests, which carry a sid rather than a tag.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: the repository writing the guidelines keeps their code out of the system's code.

decisions.problem: A push was called sharing a commit.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-pcnyfp7gev7syax: an operation of git keeps its name, so a push is called a push.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's rulings of that day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: the test's reference is its SpecTag, and what binds the symbols reads those outside the tests.

decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: The map
children.text: How the specification is drawn.

children.title: The map is a mindmap of the specification
children.text: The map is the specification seen from above: a mindmap drawn from the nodes each time it is built, holding no fact of its own. It shows the structure and the status of each node, and nothing else. The structure is a domain, the parts under it, then the rules, down to the individual rule, drawn from the nesting, the titles and the level of each domain alone. A branch opens and closes, so a reader goes to the part they came for while the whole stays in view around it. The branches read: the guidelines first, then contracts, then a branch for each level of the domains, from the top, holding its domains in the order §s-uw9n84edf7cbe9n gives, and the technical appendix last.
children.reason: A specification is read one rule at a time and has to be understood as a whole, and the two pull against each other: the full text is more than anyone holds at once, and an extract loses where the rule sits. A mindmap answers both — the shape of everything, and the detail of whatever is opened. Drawn from the nodes at each build rather than kept beside them, because a diagram kept apart is a second copy of the specification and disagrees with it silently. The levels and the order of the domains carry how the domains bear on one another. Shown on the map, the statuses tell which parts of the specification wait for their owners while the whole stays in view.

skills/tools/test/unit/generated.test.ts::@spec s-zu8ne3wq84zchc4 the map shows the structure and each node's status only, nothing of a rule's text

decisions.problem: The map showed the structure alone, so the state of the specification could not be seen at the level of its map.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the map shows each node's status.

children.title: The checks and the procedures
children.text: How a change to the specification or the code is checked, and how a procedure that writes the specification behaves.

children.title: What is checked, when, and what a failure costs
children.text:
Two things are checked mechanically: that the specification holds together on its own, and that the specification and the code still describe each other. Every check is deterministic but one: whether the code does what the nodes it names say, and nothing they do not, is judged at every commit that changes code by an independent reviewer (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). The checks run when a commit is made, and the tests of the system's code at a push while the specification is approved; each check reads the commit being made, and the history behind it where its row says so, never what the commit does not hold. A check refuses unless its row says otherwise.

**The specification on its own**

| What is checked | On failure |
|---|---|
| No file of the specification, of its archive or of its schema gives one field two values | refused |
| Every file matches its schema | refused |
| No two nodes share a sid | refused |
| No two nodes share a location | refused |
| Every node's location names where it is in the specification | refused |
| Every term node stands in contracts | refused |
| No two term nodes name the same term, whatever the case of its letters | refused |
| No two RecordTypes share a name, whatever the case of its letters | refused |
| Every node outside the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes, but a section and a domain's header, is approved only where the latest record for it and its wording's fingerprint is an approval | refused |
| Each approval a commit records names one of the owners of its node, as the commit holds them | refused |
| The status of each section and domain's header is the one the nodes under it produce | refused |
| A node a commit removes, outside the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes, is deleted where it is a section or a domain's header or no approval of it was ever given, and otherwise stands in the archive with the reason for its removal | refused |
| Every link names a node | refused |
| A node citing another holds a link to it, and a link of type cites stands only where its node cites the node it names and holds no link of another type to it | refused |
| No node cites another by its location outside text quoted as code | refused |
| A term-relation or a uses link binds two terms, and no other type of link, cites included, binds two terms | refused, and settled with the specification's owners |
| The incoming links are what the outgoing ones produce | refused |
| No approved node, and no section or domain's header, sets three words or more running in capitals outside a name quoted from the code | refused |
| Every section holds at least one rule | refused |
| Every domain has a header, and the index in it is what the domain's sections produce | refused |
| The values gathered beside a field are what their source produces | refused |
| Every domain's header names a level the project's own guidelines list | refused |
| A consumes link goes from a domain's header to a section of another domain | refused |
| An exempts link goes from a node of the project's own guidelines to a rule, a node of a project's own kind or a section | refused |
| The domains do not use one another in a cycle | refused |
| A RecordType of a domain names a RecordType of another domain only where the named RecordType stands in a section its domain's header names in its consumes links | reported by the node's sid |
| A RecordType variant refines the RecordType it is a variant of | refused |
| A RecordType variant stands in the part of the specification that declares the value it answers to | refused |
| A RecordType variant declares at least one field held neither by its RecordType nor by any field of type variant of that RecordType | refused |
| A RecordType variant answers to values of exactly the fields its RecordType names as choosing the variant, each value one its choosing field's source declares | refused |
| No two variants of one RecordType answer to the same values | refused |
| Each value of a field of type one of is declared once, the values gathered beside it not counted | refused |
| A field of type one of whose values are not those the domains add has no list a domain adds to it | refused |
| A list of values a domain adds stands in a rule of that domain refining a RecordType described in contracts, and names a field of type one of of that RecordType whose values are those the domains add | refused |
| A RecordType holds at most one field of type variant, the ones it inherits counted | refused |
| Every field of type one of holds at least one value from its source | refused |
| A field whose values are the sids of a kind's nodes names a kind of node that exists | refused |
| A field of type identifier of names a RecordType that names the field identifying it, one of its fields, and the identifying fields it leads to, followed from one identifier to the next, end in a field of another type | refused |
| Every node of the technical appendix but a section, outside the sections of the stack and of the technical debt, implements a node of the base specification, and every rule of the technical debt refines one | refused |
| Every section of the technical appendix but those of the stack and of the technical debt stands under the name of a domain | refused |
| Every rule of the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8) implements a node of the base of the guidelines | refused |
| Every rule of a project's own guidelines refines or implements a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines | refused |
| No project but the one the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in holds a copy of them or of their schema | refused |

**The specification and the code**

| What is checked | On failure |
|---|---|
| Every symbol of the system's code outside its tests carries a SpecTag naming the node it implements, or, where it implements none of the system's logic, the SpecTag that says so and gives its reason | refused, or reported by the symbol for one a commit does not change while the specification is a draft |
| A commit that makes the specification approved, where before it was a draft, leaves no symbol of the system's code outside its tests, and no test, without a SpecTag | refused |
| A commit that puts the specification back to draft records one of the specification's owners withdrawing the approval of the rule that approves it | refused |
| Every SpecTag names a node that exists, and a SpecTag on a symbol whose code a commit changes an approved one | refused |
| Every SpecTag on the code outside the tests stands on the symbol it binds | refused |
| Every test of the system's code carries the SpecTag of a rule, a term or a node of a project's own kind that exists, and a test a commit adds or changes that of an approved one | refused, or reported by the test for one carrying no SpecTag that a commit does not change while the specification is a draft |
| Every rule, or node of a project's own kind that needs code, whose code written for it a commit adds or changes has a test carrying its SpecTag | refused |
| Every test of a project's own check or generator carries the SpecTag of the rule listing it, and a test a commit adds or changes that of an approved one | refused, or reported by the test for one carrying no SpecTag that a commit does not change while the specification is a draft |
| Every project's own check or generator whose code a commit adds or changes has a test carrying the SpecTag of the rule listing it | refused |
| A node's lists of code and tests are what the SpecTags on the code and on the tests produce | refused |
| A node that names the symbols in a file is held to them | refused |
| A list a node carries matches the declaration in the code, in the schema or in the settings it names | refused |
| Each member of a list that is an object holds the property the list names | refused |
| A check a project's own guidelines add (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m) passes | refused, or reported where the rule listing it says so |
| No file the repository keeps outside the specification and the fixtures of the tests of a check reading citations or locations (§s-6hha5en226aj8hu) names a node by its location | refused |
| A citation in the code, the tests and the documents, those fixtures left out, names a node by its sid | refused |
| Every copy generated from the nodes and kept in the repository, such as the types and runtime checks of the system's code, is exactly what the nodes produce now, or, while it waits for a draft node, left unchanged by the commit: neither edited by hand nor left behind nodes that are all approved | refused |
| A copy of the system's code that waits for a draft node | reported by the node's sid |
| A rule whose tests or code lag behind its text, or whose code lags behind its tests, as the history of the repository shows | reported by the node's sid |
| An approved rule, or approved node of a project's own kind that needs code, outside the SpecSheriff guidelines, the project's own guidelines and the technical debt has a symbol and a test carrying its SpecTag, its own or that of a rule implementing it, or is exempted | reported by the node's sid |
| A commit that changes code names every approved node the SpecTags on its changed symbols outside the tests name, and no header or section | refused |
| The code does what the nodes it names say, and nothing they do not | refused, naming the node and the line |
| The tests of the system's code and of a project's own checks and generators pass | the push is refused while the specification is approved |
children.reason:
A person asking whether a commit will go through must find the whole answer in one place: spread across several rules, the answer comes apart, and one rule ends up contradicting another without anybody seeing it.

Every check but the review is binary, so refusing costs nobody a judgement, and a check that sometimes refuses for a reason nobody can reproduce is bypassed at the first chance and never trusted again. The review is the one judgement, because whether code does only what its rules say cannot be decided by a script.

A check reads the commit being made, because a judgement of anything else would pass or refuse what is not being committed. The tests run at a push rather than at a commit, since a suite takes longer than a commit should wait, and a commit not yet pushed misleads nobody.

The check of drift only reports, because a rule outrunning its tests or its code, or tests outrunning the code, is drift worth knowing about and not the fault of whoever's commit found it. An approved rule not implemented is reported rather than refused, since a rule is approved before its test and its code are written (§s-rah8b37kytb682y). A RecordType named across domains outside the sections used is reported for the reason §s-5yvpn4zhuqmv5bq gives, and a symbol or a test without a SpecTag that a commit leaves alone while the specification is a draft for the reason §s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn gives. No test runs at a push while the specification is a draft for the reason §s-xhcmchcngykvn2k gives.

decisions.problem: No check held the code to what its rules say: that was left to a review run on purpose, and none was run, so logic no rule stated reached a domain beside code that cited two checked rules.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every change to the code meets every requirement of the specification, checked at every commit by a separate, independent reviewer and by scripts that refuse logic with no reference back to the specification.

decisions.problem: The row refused a test opening with a term's sid, which §s-rah8b37kytb682y now admits, and read a test as changed where a deleted neighbour lent it the diff's lines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a changed test opens with the sid of a checked rule or term, and a test is changed when its text is.

decisions.problem: The data record nodes, and the code generated from them, had no check.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the checks of the specification hold a variant of a data record to its data record and its values to the fields that choose the variant; the binding holds the generated code to what the data record nodes produce.

decisions.problem: The checks of a data record's forms let a form hold nothing and read the values choosing a form off the forms alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record variant declares a field of its own and answers to a value declared once.

decisions.problem: The check of the appendix's implements links would have refused every rule of the technical debt, which falls short of the nodes it concerns rather than carrying them out, and debt named the binding's report of a rule outrunning its code as well.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the debt's rules are held to a refines link to a node of the base and its section to none, and the binding's report is named the drift, the word this rule's reason already used, so that debt names one thing.

decisions.problem: The table named the commands and the hooks of one toolset, and held rows only one project's specification needed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base keeps what is checked and what a failure costs; how, and by which command, is described in the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8), and a project's own rows stand in its own guidelines.

decisions.problem: Read row by row, the table left checks unclear or unmade: a term could stand in a domain with nothing refusing it, names differing only in case passed as two terms or two data records, two abbreviations side by side were refused as stress, one row joined five checks of a data record variant, and several rows named a thing without its object or read as cut off.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a term stands only in contracts; terms and data records are named once whatever the case of their letters; capitals are refused from three words running; the checks of a data record variant stand one to a row; and the rows on the appendix of the tools, the tags, addresses, generated copies and drift say what they check in full.

decisions.problem: A field of type one of could hold no value at all, and identifiers could lead from one identifying field to the next back to a data record already passed; neither has a type the implementation can be given, and nothing refused them.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's rulings of that day on where the values of a field of type one of are declared and on the type of an identifier: both are refused.

children.title: Code and tests without a SpecTag while the specification is a draft
children.text: While a project's specification is a draft, a symbol of the system's code outside its tests, or a test, that carries no SpecTag is reported rather than refused where the commit does not change it.
children.reason:
A project taking up the method holds code and tests written before its rules, which are approved only as its owners review them. A SpecTag added to a symbol, or to a test that named no node, is a change that must then name an approved node (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4, §s-rah8b37kytb682y). Refusing every symbol and test without one would refuse every commit, the project's setup included, until all of them had their rules. While the specification is a draft, the work is above all on the specification, the code and the tests secondary in it.

Only what a commit leaves alone is relieved. So no draft node is implemented, and every change to code is reviewed.

decisions.problem: A project adopting the method with code it already has could not commit while its rules were agreed, since every untagged symbol was refused and a tag added had to name a checked node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's specification is a draft or live; first, a draft relaxed every check binding the code, then, the reviewer apart finding that against two principles, narrowed: a draft relaxes only the refusal of an untagged symbol a commit does not change, which is reported; a changed symbol is held as when live.

decisions.problem: The system's code came to include its tests, which carry a sid rather than a tag.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: a symbol of the system's code outside its tests.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A project holding tests could commit nothing, its setup included, before every test named a node, though a draft relieved code without a SpecTag.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a draft is above all work on the specification, the code and the tests secondary in it; a test a commit does not change and that names no node is reported rather than refused, as code without a SpecTag is.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: Tests at a push while the specification is a draft
children.text: While a project's specification is a draft, neither the tests of the system's code nor those of the project's own checks and generators are run at a push.
children.reason: While the specification is a draft, the work is above all on the specification, the code and the tests secondary in it, and a push that waited for every test would slow that work. The tests of the project's own checks and generators go with those of the system's code, since a push runs them together (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).

decisions.problem: A push in a draft waited for every test, though a draft is above all work on the specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: while the specification is a draft, the tests need not run at a push, to keep the work quick.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: The specification's status is its owners' act
children.text:
A rule of the project's own guidelines refining this one states that the specification is approved. The specification is approved while that rule is approved, and a draft otherwise. Only the specification's owners approve that rule or withdraw its approval.

A commit that makes the specification approved, where before it was a draft, is refused unless every symbol of the system's code outside its tests, and every test, carries a SpecTag. A commit that puts it back to draft is refused unless it records one of the specification's owners withdrawing the approval of that rule.
children.reason: Whether the specification is approved decides how strictly the checks hold its code and tests (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn, §s-xhcmchcngykvn2k), so its owners decide it, both ways. They must be able to put it back to draft, whatever leads them to it. While the specification changes at its core, as when another version of it is adopted or the system's architecture changes, the code and the tests are secondary. Approved while code or tests carry no SpecTag, it would refuse the next commit for code or tests that commit did not touch. Anyone could put its rule back to draft by an edit of its wording, or remove it. So only a withdrawal by one of the specification's owners puts the specification back.

decisions.problem: Nothing said how a specification passes from a draft to live, nor who puts it there.
decisions.ruling: The owner: one marker for the whole project, set as the project takes up the method, put live by the owner, once and one way, refused while code is untagged; held as a rule of the project's own guidelines rather than a value beside the owner, since a confirmation covers a rule and no such value.

decisions.problem: The system's code came to include its tests, which carry a sid rather than a tag.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: no symbol of the system's code outside its tests is left without a tag.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A draft came to relieve a test without a SpecTag as it relieves code, while putting the specification live waited for the code alone.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn: putting it live waits for the tests as for the code.

decisions.problem: A specification was put live once and could not go back, and live was a word of its own beside a node's statuses.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification is approved or a draft, its owners' act both ways, whatever leads them to it; a commit putting it back to draft without an owner's withdrawal is refused, which covers an edit of the rule and its removal.

children.title: A project's own checks join the shared ones
children.text: A project's own guidelines may add checks, listed in a rule of theirs refining this one with what each checks and what a failure costs. Each counts among the checks of §s-jau82aq9juv9zzh: it is held to all that rule says of a check, runs wherever they run, and refuses unless that list says it reports.
children.reason: A project's own kinds of node and fields carry requirements no check of the SpecSheriff guidelines knows. Run where the shared checks run and held to what they are held to, a project's check holds every participant as they do, rather than resting on whoever remembers to run it. Listed in one rule, the project's part of whether a commit goes through stands in one place, and what a failure costs is approved by one of the specification's owners (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).

decisions.problem: A project's own rules carried requirements no check of SpecSheriff knew, and a check of its own had no place to run.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's own checks run with the shared ones, listed in one rule of its own guidelines with what each checks and what a failure costs, held to all the shared checks are held to; whether one refuses or reports is decided by that rule, which its owner confirms, and not by the settings of the tools.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: A project's own generators join the shared one
children.text: A project's own guidelines may add generators of code, listed in a rule of theirs refining this one with what each writes from which nodes. A project's generator writes the same from the same nodes, and what it writes waits for that rule as for the nodes it is written from (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).
children.reason: Code generated from a project's own kinds of node and fields is written by no generator of the SpecSheriff guidelines. A copy is checked against what its nodes produce only where the same nodes always produce the same; code from a generator whose rule is a draft implements what nobody approved (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug).

decisions.problem: Code a project generates from its own kinds and fields, as runtime checks, enumerations or a registry its runtime reads, had no generator of SpecSheriff to write it and nothing holding it to its nodes.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's own generators are listed in one rule of its own guidelines with what each writes from which nodes; what one writes is held as the generated types are, waiting for that rule as for its nodes, and the generator writes the same from the same nodes.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: A project's own checks and generators are tested against the rule listing them
children.text: Every test of a project's own check or generator carries the SpecTag of the rule listing it (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m, §s-km4x4s26kv7pjze) and is written before the code it tests. A test a commit adds or changes carries that SpecTag only once the rule is approved, and each such check or generator whose code a commit adds or changes has a test carrying it.
children.reason: A test is all that holds a project's check or generator to its rule: the code of the repository's tools is not the system's code and carries no SpecTag (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc), and what a generator writes owes no test (§s-rah8b37kytb682y) and is withheld from the reviewer (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). The rule listing a check or generator says what it checks or writes, so its tests verify that rule; a test written first tests that rule rather than what the code happened to do, and one carrying the SpecTag of a draft rule would have the code implement what nobody approved (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug).

decisions.problem: Nothing held a project's own check or generator to the rule listing it: its code carries no tag, what a generator writes owes no test and is withheld from the reviewer.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the tests of a project's own checks and generators carry the sid of the rule listing them and are written first, as the SpecSheriff tools' own tests do by the owner's choice of 2026-10-28.

decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: the code of the repository's tools is not the system's code.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's rulings of that day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: the test's reference is its SpecTag, and what binds the symbols reads those outside the tests.

decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: At a commit and at a push, the project's own tools run after the SpecSheriff tools
children.text: At a commit and at a push, the SpecSheriff tools run their checks first, and the project's own tools that run at that moment run after them. The project's own checks run among the checks of the SpecSheriff tools, not after them (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m). The project's tools run whatever the checks find, and also where the SpecSheriff tools cannot run. The commit or the push goes through only where the checks and each of the project's tools pass. None of the project's tools changes what the commit holds.
children.reason: A project may run tools of its own at a commit or a push, such as a scan that nothing internal reaches a public repository. The method governs the specification and the code bound to it (§s-efe2cmw9asrbt2g). A tool guarding anything else is the project's own concern, and taking up the method must not stop it. Such a tool makes no check of the method, so the table of checks does not list it. The SpecSheriff tools run first, since the project's tools may extend their checks but never override them. A tool that changed the commit would let through what no check read.

decisions.problem: Taking up the method set where git looks for hooks, so a project's own tools run at a commit or a push, such as a scan that nothing internal reaches a public repository, had no place to run.
decisions.ruling: The owner: at a commit and at a push the SpecSheriff tools run their checks first, then the project's own tools, whatever the checks find; both must pass. Operations of git keep their names — commit, push, merge, merge request — and the text names the SpecSheriff tools as such.

children.title: The fixtures of a check's tests are left out of the checks of citations and locations
children.text: The checks of citations and locations outside the specification leave out the files listed as fixtures of tests. The list is kept in a rule of the project's own guidelines that refines this one. It names only the fixtures of the tests of a check that reads citations or locations.
children.reason: Such a test feeds its check a file holding a sid or a location as data, not as a citation of a node. A test of any other check has no use for such a file, so the list holds no other. Listed in one rule of the project's own guidelines, the files left out are approved by one of the specification's owners (§s-67vekyup7y8smap) rather than set in the settings.

decisions.problem: A test's fixtures, holding sids and addresses as data, were refused by the scans of citations and addresses outside the specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: files listed as fixtures in a rule of the project's own guidelines are left out of those scans.

decisions.problem: Any test's fixtures could be listed and left out of the checks of citations and locations, while only a test of a check reading them needs a file holding a sid or a location as data.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the list names only the fixtures of the tests of a check that reads citations or locations.

children.title: The reviewer sees only the change and the nodes it names
children.text: The independent reviewer of a commit is given the commit's change, less the files generated from the specification, and the text and the reason of the nodes its message and the SpecTags on its symbols outside the tests name, a RecordType with its fields and a node of a project's own kind with those its kind declares (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) — and nothing of the session that wrote the code. Each file left out is named to it as holding the types and runtime checks generated from the RecordTypes, or what a project's generator wrote from the nodes it names (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze), which the check of the generated copies compares with what the nodes produce. It refuses the commit where the code does something no named node's text states or leaves out what one requires, what a RecordType requires counted as carried out by the types and runtime checks generated from it (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9) and what the rule listing a project's generator says it writes by what that generator wrote, and names the node and the line of each finding. A review that cannot be held — no reviewer to run, a run that does not end, an answer that cannot be read — refuses the commit and says why.
children.reason: Given nothing of the session that wrote the code, the reviewer reads the code against the nodes rather than against its author's intent, and a refusal naming the node and the line can be checked by anyone. A node's reason says what its rule protects, which tells the reviewer how to read a case its text leaves open. The generated files are left out because the check of the generated copies already compares them with what the nodes produce, so what a RecordType requires is decided there rather than judged. A reviewer judges what a commit leaves out only from what it is shown, so a file withheld from it, or one whose content it is not told is held elsewhere, reads to it as missing. A review that passes whenever it could not be held is a review nobody can rely on.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was given the rules a commit names and no data record, so code generated from a data record had nothing to be read against, and the definition of a term the code's names follow was withheld; a generated data record was refused field by field as stated by no rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reviewer is given the rules, data records and terms the message and the tags name, a data record with its fields.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was one agent's command line, so the method read as one vendor's tool, and a reader without that agent could not run it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base states the reviewer's contract; who carries the review out is a runner described in the appendix of the tools, and a review that cannot be held refuses the commit.

decisions.problem: The types and runtime checks generated from a project's data records are its code, so a commit adding them is reviewed, but they were left out of the change the reviewer was given without its being told so: given a message naming the data records and a change holding none of their types, the reviewer refused the commit as leaving them out.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each file left out is named to the reviewer as holding the types and runtime checks generated from the data records, which the check of the generated copies compares with what the nodes produce, and what a data record requires counts as carried out by them.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was given the fields of a data record but not those of a node of a project's own kind.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: it is given them.

decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-km4x4s26kv7pjze: it is told of what a project's generator wrote, and counts what its rule says it writes as carried out by it.

decisions.ruling: The owner: it is given each node's reason too, and refuses only what no named node's text states.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's rulings of that day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: the test's reference is its SpecTag, and what binds the symbols reads those outside the tests.

children.title: A procedure that writes the specification is idempotent
children.text: Every procedure that writes the specification, or what is generated from it, is idempotent: run again on what its previous run left, it gives the same result and changes nothing, so running it again is always safe. A procedure needed only once, such as bringing existing documents into the model, is removed once it is done, since it is idempotent only on the state of the specification it was written for.
children.reason: Whoever works on the specification may run such a procedure at any time, by hand or as part of a check, without knowing whether it has run before; one whose second run changed anything would damage the specification the next time it ran. A procedure written for one state of the specification can damage a later one.

decisions.problem: Safety to run again was stated of the commands of one toolset, in words that did not name the property they meant.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is stated of every procedure that writes the specification, by its standard name, idempotent.

children.title: Where an agent writes, the checks run at each of its edits
children.text:
Where an agent writes the specification, the tests or the code, the checks of the specification and of the code run after each of its edits, and what they refuse is reported to the agent.

Before an edit is made, it is refused where it would leave a node approved, a section and a domain's header left out, over a wording for which no approval stands (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq), change the code written for a rule, or for a node of a project's own kind that needs code (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), that no test carries the SpecTag of (§s-rah8b37kytb682y), change the code of a project's own check or generator while no test carries the SpecTag of the rule listing it (§s-sfjka4zc4rhfu67), or change the approvals otherwise than through the procedure that records an approval or withdraws one.
children.reason:
An agent told of a refusal at the edit that caused it mends it there, rather than at the commit among every other.

A node is approved by one of its owners, or in that owner's name by the agent working for them where its change states nothing new (§s-67vekyup7y8smap). So an agent that could set a status, or write an approval itself, could approve what none of its owners agreed to. Every later check takes the approvals as given, so they can be held only where they are written. The procedure that records an approval takes the wording the node already holds and refuses an approval by anyone who is none of the node's owners, and a withdrawal only makes a node a draft.

A commit holds a test and its code together whichever was written first, so the order of the work can be held only where the edits are made.

decisions.problem: The checks ran only at a commit: an agent met every refusal at once, far from the edits that caused them, nothing held the order of rule, test and code that a commit cannot show, and a status an agent set was caught only at the commit.
decisions.ruling: The owner: where an agent writes, the checks run at each of its edits, and an edit that would leave a node checked unconfirmed or change the code of a rule with no test is refused before it is made; the hooks ship with the tools and are kept in git.

decisions.problem: An agent could write a confirmation of a new wording into the confirmations and then reword a checked node: the check before the edit found the confirmation and let the edit pass, and only this rule's reason spoke against it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an agent's edit changing the confirmations is refused before it is made; only the procedure that records a confirmation or withdraws one writes them.

decisions.problem: The reason held that nobody but a node's owner confirms it, while the agent working for the owner may now confirm in the owner's name a node whose change states nothing new.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-67vekyup7y8smap: the reason names that exception.

decisions.problem: The guard held only a rule's code to a test written first.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: it holds the code written for a node of a project's own kind that needs code as well.

decisions.problem: The guard held only the system's code to a test written first.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-sfjka4zc4rhfu67: it holds the code of a project's own checks and generators so too.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's rulings of that day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: the test's reference is its SpecTag, and what binds the symbols reads those outside the tests.

decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

children.title: How a rule is written
children.text: How a node of the specification is written.

children.title: The specification is written in English
children.text: Every node of the specification is written in English, and so is everything generated from the nodes. A quotation, such as a name from the code or a text the system shows its users, keeps the language of what it quotes.
children.reason:
A specification that mixes two languages, in its nodes or in what is generated from them and read in their place, loses the line between what it states and what is an aside.

The language is English because a project's guidelines include the SpecSheriff guidelines, which a project takes as they are written and never changes (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), and those are written in English: a project's own nodes in another language would mix two languages in one specification. English is also the language the readers of a specification are likeliest to share.

A quotation must match what it quotes letter for letter, and, standing apart from the words around it, it does not blur what the node states.

decisions.problem: The rule named English, a choice one project made for its readers, which another project's readers need not share.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification is written in one language, English being recommended and holding where a project's own guidelines name no other; the SpecSheriff guidelines themselves are written in English.

decisions.problem: The rule let a project's owner name another language for the specification and required everything generated from its nodes to be in it, while a project's guidelines include the SpecSheriff guidelines, written in English, and no field held the language named for a tool to write in it the words it adds to what it generates, such as the labels of the export and of the map; and the one language held a node's quotations too, though a name from the code or a text the system shows its users may be in another.
decisions.ruling: The owner: everything of SpecSheriff is in English, every project's specification included; a quotation keeps the language of what it quotes.

children.title: A rule names its subject and states what must hold
children.text: A rule names the subject it binds and states what that subject must do: not “credentials are kept encrypted”, which binds nobody, but “the store of secrets keeps every credential encrypted”. A property is stated over what the specification declares, never over what happens not to exist yet: not “a timestamp needs no time zone while every user is in one”, but “a timestamp carries its time zone”. A rule of the technical debt names its subject the same way and states what that subject does while the problem stands (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).
children.reason: Such a sentence is true when it is written and silently false afterwards: nothing breaks, no check can fire, and the next reader takes an observation for an obligation. Naming the subject is also what makes a rule gradeable at all, since a requirement with nobody to hold it is one nobody can be found to have broken. A rule of the technical debt describes on purpose, and is removed with its problem (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

decisions.problem: A rule of the technical debt states what its subject does while a problem stands, which this rule's demand that a rule state what its subject must do did not admit.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the exception is written here, where the rule it narrows is read.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

children.title: A name is quoted where the reader must reach it, a predicate where the rule must keep binding
children.text: Where a rule binds a named thing, the name is quoted where the reader must reach the definition that owns it, and the predicate is stated where the rule must keep binding if that name changes: not “`deleted_users` is never searched”, which binds nothing once the table is renamed, but “a table holding the users who deleted their accounts — today `deleted_users` — is never searched”.
children.reason: A sentence written against a name goes inert rather than failing when the name moves: nothing breaks, no test moves, and a requirement quietly becomes a statement about nothing. A sentence written against the predicate keeps binding whatever the thing is called, and is useless exactly where the reader needs to find the definition.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

children.title: A reason is no narrower than the rule it holds up
children.text: A node's reason covers everything the node's text requires: a rule that refuses an upload too large to store and tells the user why gives a reason for both, not only for the refusal. Where the reason is narrower, either the reason is completed or the rule is cut back to what the reason carries.
children.reason: A rule with a narrow reason is destroyed by the next author doing everything right: the change is checked against the stated reason, the reason still holds, and the property nobody wrote down is gone. A reviewer cannot defend what the node never said.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

children.title: A reason gives its grounds and nothing more
children.text: A reason states the ground its rule rests on, as a rule in its first sentence. Beyond that ground, a reason carries only a caveat for a case the ground does not reach, and further grounds that do not overlap it; what a mistake would cost and a restatement of the rule's text are left out.
children.reason: Whatever a reason says beyond its grounds blurs them, until a reader can no longer tell which sentence the rule rests on. And a rule held up by grounds that do not overlap survives any one of them going stale.

children.title: No count in prose
children.text: A node states no count of what the specification or a registry holds — of nodes, of states, of members, of commands — and a sentence correcting a count is a count. Where the number matters, it is produced by whatever holds the set: not “contracts holds 45 nodes”, which was true for one day, but the figure counted off the model each time it is shown.
children.reason: A count is a second copy of a fact, and the copy is the one that goes stale. It goes stale silently and in the direction that reads as correct, because a number that is merely out of date looks exactly like a number that is right.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/generated.test.ts::@spec s-xtqebaxjrqjsjwn sheriff guide prints every node of the guidelines and the figures counted off the model as it prints

children.title: A restriction by list is chosen by which mistake would go unnoticed
children.text: Where a rule restricts something by a list, it says whether the list names what is allowed or what is forbidden, and chooses by which mistake would go unnoticed: where something left out would go unnoticed, the list names what is forbidden, as the records a backup leaves out; where something let in would go unnoticed, it names what is allowed, as the fields a public API returns.
children.reason: A list goes wrong on whatever nobody thought of when it was written: one naming what is allowed shuts out every newcomer, one naming what is forbidden lets every newcomer in, and for a given restriction only one of those two mistakes is noticed.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: The rule spoke of sets, where what a rule does is restrict something by a list, and spent its words on what everyone knows of allow-lists and deny-lists rather than on how to choose between them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it speaks of a restriction by list and keeps the criterion for choosing one.

children.title: A general word carries its object
children.text: A rule names the concrete thing it means rather than a general word for it: not “a limit on how many records a listing shows”, which also let an export drop records, but “a limit on how many records a user interface shows”. Where a general word cannot be avoided — a model, a structure, a check — it carries its object in the same phrase: the structure of which record, the check at which moment comparing what with what, the model of what. A name the specification defines — a term, a RecordType, a field — is never a general word alone, such as type, action or item, but carries its object: userAction, not action.
children.reason: A rule has no conversation around it to supply a missing object, and a general rule has the least context of all, so every reader supplies an object of their own and the rule binds whatever each of them chose. Nothing about the word itself looks wrong, which is why the ambiguity survives every reading. A defined name is read in every rule that uses it, far from its definition, and a general one there means whatever each rule's context suggests: a field called type held a kind of request in one log, a user's action in another and a kind of error in a third.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: The schema of a node names several of its fields type and one kind, general words this rule keeps a name the specification defines from being.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a field of the node schema is read within the object holding it, which carries its object, so the schema keeps type and kind.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

children.title: No phrase or sentence is set in capitals
children.text: A node is written in the ordinary case of its language, and a name quoted from the code keeps its spelling. Outside such a name, capitals may stand on one word or on two running (REST API); a phrase or a sentence, three words or more running, is never set in capitals: what must stand out is said in the words.
children.reason: Set in capitals, a phrase reads as more binding than the words around it, although every word of a rule binds alike, and a reader who meets capitals on every line starts reading the capitals instead of the sentence. A style spreads by imitation, because a rule is written like the rules around it, so one rule in capitals is copied by its neighbours. A word or two in capitals are most often an abbreviation or a name keeping its own spelling, which no check tells from a word stressed, so they are left alone. Three words running are seldom anything but stress, and a run of abbreviations as long is rare enough to be worded around.

decisions.problem: The check refused two words in capitals running, so two abbreviations side by side, such as REST API, were refused as stress although this rule let an abbreviation keep its capitals; and a single word stressed in capitals, which this rule forbade, no check could tell from an abbreviation.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a single word, or two running, may stand in capitals; a phrase or a sentence, from three words running, never does.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/validate.test.ts::@spec s-m6upmfq64kw5h4r refuses three words or more running in capitals, letters beyond ASCII included, two words left out

children.title: What no rule requires is not done
children.text: Whatever no rule requires is not done, and needs no rule saying so. Where a rule's words would also cover a case they must not, the exception is written into that rule, so that the rule is exact where it is read.
children.reason: A prohibition that answers no rule decides nothing, and each one written suggests that whatever it does not name is allowed. An exception kept apart from the rule it narrows is missed by whoever reads the rule alone.

decisions.problem: A rule binding every store of one kind fitted a store for which it had nothing worth measuring, and a rule saying only that something is not done had been proposed for it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: what no rule requires is understood as not done and needs no rule; an exception refining a general rule is written, for the rule to be exact.
